In the movie _Wall Street_ , Gordon Gekko famously declares that "greed is good." But there is another g-word that the actual Wall Street might also love, and it isn't greed. It's gridlock. Not the kind on the Long Island Expressway or on Route 93 entering Boston at rush hour. The kind in Washington where one party holds the White House and the other holds at least one chamber of Congress. For most of the last century, that has been the market's preferred form of government. And it may be about to get it once again.
With two days to go until the midterms, prediction markets on Kalshi and Polymarket give Democrats roughly a 90% or better chance of taking the House and something in the mid-to-high 60s for the Senate. The single most likely outcome priced by both markets is a full Democratic sweep of Congress, at around 70% at the time of this writing. (_See below for real time updates on the current prediction market percentages_.) If that holds, the Trump administration goes from unified control to divided government for the first time, and investors betting on legislative paralysis will be grinning.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/8bcc8e47-3c77-419e-93f0-aa5698247dab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Why? Because a divided government seems to suggest higher returns. Ned Davis Research tracked returns of the Dow Jones Index by government configuration going back to 1901. Divided governments, where at least one chamber of Congress is held by the opposing party, returned an annualized 8.0%. Unified governments returned 4.0%. _Double!_
When you break it down further, the picture gets more interesting. Unified Republican government, like we have had for the past two years, is the worst of all four possibilities, at just 1.54% annualized. A Republican president with a Democratic Congress? 6.37%, more than four times the return. The best configuration of all is a Democratic president checked by a Republican Congress, at 9.60%. The market doesn't love any particular party. It loves the restraint that comes when neither party can do whatever it wants.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/87ac0593-f81e-4ba4-a15d-82f920ad3a89?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
To be fair, there are numerous interpretations. This is far from a settled science. A pair of Oxford economists sliced the data differently, using data from 1927 to 2017 and found the opposite: unified governments have produced higher stock returns and faster growth. Average the whole century and the two camps roughly cancel out, which might by itself be the point. Over the long sweep, party control explains far less about markets than investors assume. **What matters is the starting point, and the starting point today is a unified government that has been pulling hard on every lever at once.**
[](https://substack.com/redirect/24b05291-3dca-4cbc-ae88-ad600e31a0ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
So how do unified and divided governments differ with respect to key economic indicators like growth and inequality?
On**growth** , there doesn't seem to be much difference. Kevin Hassett, now a senior Trump economic adviser, ran the numbers back in 2010 and found that since 1970, median real GDP growth was 3.3% in years of divided government versus 3.0% under one-party rule, with median unemployment of 5.7% versus 6.1%. On the margin, divided government outperforms, albeit only slightly. Wall Street compounded the small difference into larger financial market differences. The S&P 500 rose a median 13.5% a year under divided government against 9% when one party ruled.
One consistent finding that is quite powerful, however, is that divided governments slow the growth of federal spending. Turns out the government shrinks as a share of GDP only when control is split, and that division is a necessary, if not sufficient, condition for fiscal restraint. The three balanced budgets of the late 1990s were produced by a Democratic president and a Republican Congress that could agree on little else. And given today's runaway debt and ballooning deficits, this really matters.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/00e2e211-6966-40b9-ad08-095b043f2fb7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
So when I summarize the evidence as I read it, it seems the economy grows marginally faster under a divided government and, perhaps more importantly, doesn't whipsaw as much. Uncertainty falls. When a unified government can plausibly rewrite trade policy, tax policy and industrial policy in a single session, every capital-spending decision bears an uncertainty premium. Remove the possibility of rapid sweeping change and that premium collapses. Businesses don't need Washington to help. They need to know Washington will stay out of the way and leave them alone.
When it comes to **inequality** , the data is pretty clear. Unified Democratic control in Washington pushes the top-1% share down over time; unified Republican control pushes it up. Divided government sits in between, which is to say it leaves the distribution roughly where it was prior to the divided government getting sworn in.
The implication is that divided government is a hedge against redistribution risk in both directions. The past two years delivered tax cuts whose benefits flowed disproportionately to capital, alongside tariffs that function as a regressive consumption tax on labor and everyone else. A Democratic Congress cannot reverse either without the president's signature. But it can block the next round.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/ece09dbb-fdfa-441c-8f96-09f208dcfb2d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The common belief that divided government means nothing gets done isn't quite accurate. It's probably better to say nothing _overtly partisan_ gets done, but what does get done is usually consequential. Consider what has gotten done during divided governments over the last 50 years. The 1983 Social Security rescue, negotiated by Ronald Reagan and Tip O'Neill. The 1986 Tax Reform Act, the last time Washington actually simplified the code. The 1990 Clean Air Act amendments and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Welfare reform in 1996 and the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. The 2015 highway bill and the 2018 criminal justice reform.
Interestingly, none of this legislation was anyone's first choice. All of them stuck, because legislation that needs both parties to pass tends to survive the next election, whereas legislation passed on a party-line vote gets re-litigated the moment the majority flips.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..qIqrH58m5QbF107JDZQGDHKVJ8qLUpBO8JcA1FhI96w?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=222957196)
So on the margin, the gridlock of divided government is probably good, right? Maybe. It depends. As I noted above, the starting point matters. So let's look at where we stand after two years of a unified government:
* Tariffs that the Tax Foundation estimates cost the average household roughly $1,000 last year and another $820 this year, with the New York Fed finding that businesses and consumers absorbed nearly 90% of the burden.
* Diesel at $6.35 a gallon as of the Energy Department's latest weekly survey, a record and up $2.63 from a year ago. A war with Iran that has kept the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial traffic for more than 240 days, with Brent at $113.
* A Federal Reserve that held rates at 3.75% to 4% this week and could not cut, with two officials dissenting in favor of a hike because inflation won't cooperate.
* A 10-year Treasury that touched 5.2% earlier this month, a level unseen since 2007, and a 30-year still above 5.3%.
* And a stock market so stretched that the Buffett Indicator, total market capitalization to GDP, sits somewhere between 233% and 244% depending on who is counting, the highest ever recorded. At the dot-com peak it was roughly 140%. We are _way above_ the previous bubble.

A Democratic Congress can't really fix any of this, at least not quickly. It won't bring diesel back to $3 or immediately end the war. But it can do something important: it can stop making things worse. No new tariffs. No more blank-check spending on AI subsidies or military adventures. No active industrial policy that crowns national champions. In the current environment, the most bullish thing Washington can do is nothing.
Bloomberg Intelligence's Mike McGlone recently drew a scary parallel to the Hoover era: Market cap at about 2.5 times GDP, commodities surging, a Federal Reserve tightening into what may be the late innings of a cycle.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/e1b1848f-62a3-41e4-924f-35248ad664cb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
It is the kind of comparison nobody wants to make, and everybody should. _It 's probably prudent to ask: Are we headed into a Depression? And if so, will that create a unification of purpose, even among a divided government?_
Some will say divided government means no progress on deficit reduction, no structural reform, just two years of posturing before 2028. That may be true. _**But we are past the point where Washington needs to do something. We are at the point where it needs to stop doing things**_. Stop pouring fiscal gasoline on an inflationary fire. Stop starting trade wars. Stop starting real wars. The market doesn't need leadership from Washington right now. It needs a breather.
* * *
## [The Canary in the Frozen Food Aisle](https://substack.com/redirect/dde8fb15-ab63-4ca1-ab0d-d7726385f422?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

Frozen pizza isn't a product. It's a signal. And right now, the signal is flashing red.](https://substack.com/redirect/dde8fb15-ab63-4ca1-ab0d-d7726385f422?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

* * *
I keep coming back to a line from the late MIT economist Rudiger Dornbusch: in economics, things take longer to happen than you think they will, and then they happen faster than you thought they could. The Buffett Indicator above 230%. Diesel at records. Bitcoin at $77,000, nearly 40% below its peak. Gold down 27% from its January high, and yet long Treasuries still yielding more than 5%. These are not signs of stability.
Readers know that the core theme of my work is how to navigate uncertainty. Unified governments create a lot of it, because they can act unilaterally and do many things whose ramifications they can barely fathom. That makes navigation more challenging. Divided governments find little they can agree on and little they can actually get done...which suggests whatever does get done is well-vetted, important, and usually durable.
While it's impossible to know if we're heading towards a more certain environment, Tuesday's midterm results will definitely shed some light on how the next two years will feel.

Why Wall Street might be rooting for a divided Washington on November 3rd. | | | Nov 1 | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- In the movie Wall Street , Gordon Gekko famously declares that "greed is good." But there is another g-word that the actual Wall Street might also love, and it isn't greed. It's gridlock. Not the kind on the Long Island Expressway or on Route 93 entering Boston at rush hour. The kind in Washington where one party holds the White House and the other holds at least one chamber of Congress. For most of the last century, that has been the market's preferred form of government. And it may be about to get it once again. With two days to go until the midterms, prediction markets on Kalshi and Polymarket give Democrats roughly a 90% or better chance of taking the House and something in the mid-to-high 60s for the Senate. The single most likely outcome priced by both markets is a full Democratic sweep of Congress, at around 70% at the time of this writing. (See below for real time updates on the current prediction market percentages.) If that holds, the Trump administration goes from unified control to divided government for the first time, and investors betting on legislative paralysis will be grinning. Why? Because a divided government seems to suggest higher returns. Ned Davis Research tracked returns of the Dow Jones Index by government configuration going back to 1901. Divided governments, where at least one chamber of Congress is held by the opposing party, returned an annualized 8.0%. Unified governments returned 4.0%. Double! When you break it down further, the picture gets more interesting. Unified Republican government, like we have had for the past two years, is the worst of all four possibilities, at just 1.54% annualized. A Republican president with a Democratic Congress? 6.37%, more than four times the return. The best configuration of all is a Democratic president checked by a Republican Congress, at 9.60%. The market doesn't love any particular party. It loves the restraint that comes when neither party can do whatever it wants. To be fair, there are numerous interpretations. This is far from a settled science. A pair of Oxford economists sliced the data differently, using data from 1927 to 2017 and found the opposite: unified governments have produced higher stock returns and faster growth. Average the whole century and the two camps roughly cancel out, which might by itself be the point. Over the long sweep, party control explains far less about markets than investors assume. What matters is the starting point, and the starting point today is a unified government that has been pulling hard on every lever at once. So how do unified and divided governments differ with respect to key economic indicators like growth and inequality? Ongrowth , there doesn't seem to be much difference. Kevin Hassett, now a senior Trump economic adviser, ran the numbers back in 2010 and found that since 1970, median real GDP growth was 3.3% in years of divided government versus 3.0% under one-party rule, with median unemployment of 5.7% versus 6.1%. On the margin, divided government outperforms, albeit only slightly. Wall Street compounded the small difference into larger financial market differences. The S&P 500 rose a median 13.5% a year under divided government against 9% when one party ruled. One consistent finding that is quite powerful, however, is that divided governments slow the growth of federal spending. Turns out the government shrinks as a share of GDP only when control is split, and that division is a necessary, if not sufficient, condition for fiscal restraint. The three balanced budgets of the late 1990s were produced by a Democratic president and a Republican Congress that could agree on little else. And given today's runaway debt and ballooning deficits, this really matters. So when I summarize the evidence as I read it, it seems the economy grows marginally faster under a divided government and, perhaps more importantly, doesn't whipsaw as much. Uncertainty falls. When a unified government can plausibly rewrite trade policy, tax policy and industrial policy in a single session, every capital-spending decision bears an uncertainty premium. Remove the possibility of rapid sweeping change and that premium collapses. Businesses don't need Washington to help. They need to know Washington will stay out of the way and leave them alone. When it comes to inequality , the data is pretty clear. Unified Democratic control in Washington pushes the top-1% share down over time; unified Republican control pushes it up. Divided government sits in between, which is to say it leaves the distribution roughly where it was prior to the divided government getting sworn in. The implication is that divided government is a hedge against redistribution risk in both directions. The past two years delivered tax cuts whose benefits flowed disproportionately to capital, alongside tariffs that function as a regressive consumption tax on labor and everyone else. A Democratic Congress cannot reverse either without the president's signature. But it can block the next round. The common belief that divided government means nothing gets done isn't quite accurate. It's probably better to say nothing overtly partisan gets done, but what does get done is usually consequential. Consider what has gotten done during divided governments over the last 50 years. The 1983 Social Security rescue, negotiated by Ronald Reagan and Tip O'Neill. The 1986 Tax Reform Act, the last time Washington actually simplified the code. The 1990 Clean Air Act amendments and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Welfare reform in 1996 and the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. The 2015 highway bill and the 2018 criminal justice reform. Interestingly, none of this legislation was anyone's first choice. All of them stuck, because legislation that needs both parties to pass tends to survive the next election, whereas legislation passed on a party-line vote gets re-litigated the moment the majority flips. So on the margin, the gridlock of divided government is probably good, right? Maybe. It depends. As I noted above, the starting point matters. So let's look at where we stand after two years of a unified government: Tariffs that the Tax Foundation estimates cost the average household roughly $1,000 last year and another $820 this year, with the New York Fed finding that businesses and consumers absorbed nearly 90% of the burden. Diesel at $6.35 a gallon as of the Energy Department's latest weekly survey, a record and up $2.63 from a year ago. A war with Iran that has kept the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial traffic for more than 240 days, with Brent at $113. A Federal Reserve that held rates at 3.75% to 4% this week and could not cut, with two officials dissenting in favor of a hike because inflation won't cooperate. A 10-year Treasury that touched 5.2% earlier this month, a level unseen since 2007, and a 30-year still above 5.3%. And a stock market so stretched that the Buffett Indicator, total market capitalization to GDP, sits somewhere between 233% and 244% depending on who is counting, the highest ever recorded. At the dot-com peak it was roughly 140%. We are way above the previous bubble. A Democratic Congress can't really fix any of this, at least not quickly. It won't bring diesel back to $3 or immediately end the war. But it can do something important: it can stop making things worse. No new tariffs. No more blank-check spending on AI subsidies or military adventures. No active industrial policy that crowns national champions. In the current environment, the most bullish thing Washington can do is nothing. Bloomberg Intelligence's Mike McGlone recently drew a scary parallel to the Hoover era: Market cap at about 2.5 times GDP, commodities surging, a Federal Reserve tightening into what may be the late innings of a cycle. It is the kind of comparison nobody wants to make, and everybody should. It 's probably prudent to ask: Are we headed into a Depression? And if so, will that create a unification of purpose, even among a divided government? Some will say divided government means no progress on deficit reduction, no structural reform, just two years of posturing before 2028. That may be true. But we are past the point where Washington needs to do something. We are at the point where it needs to stop doing things. Stop pouring fiscal gasoline on an inflationary fire. Stop starting trade wars. Stop starting real wars. The market doesn't need leadership from Washington right now. It needs a breather. | | | | ---|---|--- | Oct 11 | I keep coming back to a line from the late MIT economist Rudiger Dornbusch: in economics, things take longer to happen than you think they will, and then they happen faster than you thought they could. The Buffett Indicator above 230%. Diesel at records. Bitcoin at $77,000, nearly 40% below its peak. Gold down 27% from its January high, and yet long Treasuries still yielding more than 5%. These are not signs of stability. Readers know that the core theme of my work is how to navigate uncertainty. Unified governments create a lot of it, because they can act unilaterally and do many things whose ramifications they can barely fathom. That makes navigation more challenging. Divided governments find little they can agree on and little they can actually get done...which suggests whatever does get done is well-vetted, important, and usually durable. While it's impossible to know if we're heading towards a more certain environment, Tuesday's midterm results will definitely shed some light on how the next two years will feel. | | ---|---|--- VIKRAM MANSHARAMANI is an entrepreneur, consultant, scholar, neighbor, husband, father, volunteer, and professional generalist who thinks in multiple-dimensions and looks beyond the short-term. name: Sen. Jeff Bridges
subject: Mayor Pete's first campaign wasn't for president
body:
Pete Buttigieg told a packed room how hard it is to get people excited about a State Treasurer's race. He would know. He ran for Indiana Treasurer

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/4b7f424d0f73/get-more-smarter-on-colorados-budget-10379931?e=b48bb2b4f4)
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/SZth39NoFq_?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8)
| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | Hi there,
On Wednesday in Highlands Ranch, Pete Buttigieg told a packed room how hard it is to get people excited about a State Treasurer's race. He would know. He ran for Indiana State Treasurer in 2010.
**I shouted back, "The most important office in the state!" Everyone laughed. I was only kind of joking.**
Congressman Joe Neguse, who grew up in Highlands Ranch, joined us alongside longtime Douglas County Democrats. Having grown up in Arapahoe County, I know what it’s like when red counties turn blue. This is their year.
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/Tk5CzSX1kPX?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8)
| | Nobody talks about faith and governing better than Pete.
I've long believed a budget is a moral document. It puts in dollars and cents exactly what we value and how much. The same goes for our investments, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
**That's why the Treasurer's office matters. We can put Colorado dollars to work in Colorado to build homes people can afford, renewable energy that lowers bills, and child care that doesn't cost more than rent.**
Pete told me he appreciated how I explained why the Treasurer's office matters. He'd struggled with that when he ran. I told him things seem to have worked out pretty well for him all the same.
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/s6yBLqa9Fe2?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8)
| | It's too late to mail your ballot! Use an official drop box or voting center by 7 p.m. Tuesday, November 3.
[Find your nearest ballot drop box here.](https://us.list-manage.com/6FA89VYQjwH?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8) And if you’ve already voted, make sure your friends and family vote, too!
Talk soon,
ps We lost Captain Picard this week. Pete is a huge Star Trek nerd, and when he guest-hosted _Jimmy Kimmel_ , he interviewed Sir Patrick Stewart, who surprised him with an original Star Trek script. [It's worth a watch.](https://us.list-manage.com/7s1vT_HZykr?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8) Godspeed, Captain.
---

body:
A message from the campaign trail.

| | | | | | | Because rural Minnesotans deserve nice things.
---

[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/erbawL1Ml67?e=af2b1072ff&c2id=7b6b222af6ad8adb2a2d188cd2154c87)
| | | | | |

# **Why we are voting for Reed!**
---
|
---
| |
# “Reed is the kinda guy that shows up.”
_-Amy Karwoski_
---
| | Reed was one of the first people I met after arriving in Bemidji from NYC. Shortly after meeting at the public library, he offered me a spare AC unit for my sweltering rental. To my surprise, he returned with it a few minutes later.
Fast-forward 7 years, and we have spent 4 of them working together– as the administrative wing of the _Nameless Coalition for the Homeless_ and also as his current campaign coordinator. During this time, I have gotten to know Reed as**a leader, an advocate, a problem solver, a public servant, a visionary, a squeaky wheel, a canary in the coal mine, an empath and a loyal friend** to many.
---
| | | | | | | | | | |
---
| |
---
| | **I can attest that Reed is the kinda guy who:**
-Drives you to a doctor appt. during a busy workday-Takes care of your cat when you have to leave town-Agrees to dress up with you for Halloween so you don’t feel stupid-Calls the AG when you are fighting with your bank-Drops off homemade bone broth when you are sick-Continuously fixes your fishing pole-Encourages you to become a more informed, powerful version of yourself-Is your emergency contact because he is actually the most likely to show up
I have watched Reed advocate for hundreds of individuals over the years, as county commissioner and as non-profit director (for years without pay). He treats every person he meets like family. He brings the same kinetic energy to every problem and the same pugnacious creativity to every solution.
**I trust Reed to be my elected representative.**
I feel strongly enough about getting Reed elected that I agreed to join his campaign full-time. I have benefitted greatly from his friendship over the years and I want to live in a world where all my neighbors have a guy like him in their corner.
Reed is the kinda guy that shows up.
**He will be the representative that shows up for you.**
_Amy Karwoski_ Campaign ManagerVote Reed Olson

| | | Hi there, it's Martin Sheen. I know seeing my name in your inbox might come as a surprise, but I need to talk to you about the country we both love ‐‐ and why I hope you'll fight for it alongside me.

If you don't have time to hear my whole pitch, here's my ask: [**Will you join me in the fight for our future by donating $7 _(generously matched to $35)_ to help my friends at the DSCC take back the Senate for Democrats?**](https://go.dscc.org/go/24502?amount=7&t=5&firstname=&lastname=&email=dpwillis67%40gmail.com&addr1=&addr2=&city=Cresco&state=Pennsylvania&zip=18326&phone=None&employer=&occupation=&ask=7&amounts=7%2C14%2C28%2C70&code=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&refcode=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&akid=27274%2E9716520%2E6ykqz8)

You see, I was once the "acting" president of the United States ‐‐ and while I may have been playing a fictional role, the lessons I learned were very real.

I'll let you in on the most important one: **Every person has the power to make a difference.**

You might find that hard to believe right now, after everything we've seen and endured in the past two years.

I certainly wouldn't blame you for feeling that way.

But look beyond the terrible headlines, and you might just see what I see: Americans of every background and belief, standing up in ways big and small, _sacrificing_ to bring about a future better than our present.

Whether they succeed is, in part, up to you.

One seemingly small action you can take to help is to join with your fellow Democrats and pitch in $7 to help elect a Democratic Senate majority.

Flipping the Senate and bringing accountability to this administration _will_ make a difference, but it will only be possible if we lock hands, raise our voices, and come together ‐‐ that's when we can accomplish truly incredible things.

**The headwinds we face are strong, but we are stronger. Donald Trump is determined, but we are more determined. And right now, as we stretch our arms toward the future, I hope you'll join me.**

[**I'm coming to you humbly: Before the midnight deadline passes, will you contribute $7 to the DSCC as we take the next step together? Thanks to help from a kind group of donors, we're unlocking a _quintuple ‐impact match_ so your gift will go five times as far!**](https://go.dscc.org/go/24502?amount=7&t=6&firstname=&lastname=&email=dpwillis67%40gmail.com&addr1=&addr2=&city=Cresco&state=Pennsylvania&zip=18326&phone=None&employer=&occupation=&ask=7&amounts=7%2C14%2C28%2C70&code=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&refcode=DPE-FD-20261101-MartinSheen-WhatASKMeans2026RF-Pros-sl1&akid=27274%2E9716520%2E6ykqz8)

Hey there, it's Troy.

I had to pull over and reach out as soon as I could. My campaign manager, Hilary, just called me with some pretty ugly news:

We're falling far behind our must-reach midnight fundraising goal **with just 2** **days** **until the** **election**. And it's not just your usual slow period -- we're at a point where we need to consider cutting a day of TV ads.

It may not sound like much, but going dark for even a day would be brutal. There are still 5% of undecided voters that I have to reach! And if we don't, Susan Collins will have the airwaves to herself.

**[So before I get back on the road, will you please take 2 minutes to donate $15 to help us reach our goal and keep our ads on the air? We need a massive push to get back on track! You can donate using the button below.](https://substack.com/redirect/1059d538-6199-4555-8bda-a9ba027fea7d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**

Thank you for everything!
\- Troy

body:

Peter, we’re two days from Election Day, and I wanted to be sure to **thank you for being part of this team.**
It’s thanks to your dedication to what we’re doing together that we were able to hit our October fundraising goals. It’s thanks to your generosity that we’re headed into the final hours ready to build on the progress we’ve already made for Maryland. And it’s thanks to your determination that we’re going to leave no one behind.
**Together, we’ll continue that mission.** If you’re ready to help us win, **[I would appreciate a contribution today.](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261101-2.NXh7Z_&refcode=em-20261101-2&t=2&akid=2238%2E1086043%2EX-494r)**
More soon.
Elevate,
Wes

**[Volunteer »](https://support.wesmoore.com/a/volunteer?source=em-20261101-2)**

BY AUTHORITY: WES MOORE FOR MARYLAND, MARY TYDINGS, TREASURER
